extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, regulatory/compliance professionals, and industry counsel for FDA-regulated diagnostic companies
extracted.subtask_description: Case summary and regulatory-analysis of the criminal prosecutions of Theranos executives, focusing on the factual allegations, regulatory inspection findings (FDA/CMS), patient impact, enforcement outcomes, and implications for oversight of diagnostics (LDTs/IVDs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wire fraud and conspiracy charges (18 U.S.C. §1343, §1349)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendants were charged with two counts of conspiracy to commit wire fraud (18 U.S.C. §1349) and nine counts of wire fraud (18 U.S.C. §1343) for making false statements to investors, doctors, and patients about the performance of Theranos’ blood testing technology and the Company’s financial and business prospects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegations include false advertising claims about test accuracy, speed, cost, capability to run many tests from a fingerstick, false statements about business relationships (Walgreens, DoD), false representations of regulatory status and validations, and fabricated demonstrations. The charging theory focused on misrepresentations used to induce purchases and investments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admitting regulatory violations as evidence of state of mind/intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Court permitted introduction of FDA, CMS, and CDPH inspection reports and related evidence to show Holmes' state of mind, knowledge, and intent regarding Theranos’ compliance and whether she intended to mislead investors about test accuracy and reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory-violation evidence was allowed not as proof of regulatory guilt per se but as probative of the defendants’ knowledge and intent tied to the fraud counts; jury instructed to consider such evidence only in light of elements charged in the indictment.

rubrics_metrics.name: CLIA compliance requirements — quality control (QC) and quality assessment (QA)
rubrics_metrics.description: CLIA conditions require acceptable quality control and implementation of QA procedures to identify and correct problems when systems fail precision requirements and to correct QC program issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS report cited failure to ensure acceptable QC prior to reporting patient results, failure to institute QA to identify/correct problems, and examples where large percentages of QC samples flagged inability to produce accurate results. These are core CLIA performance expectations for laboratories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate jeopardy determination under 42 C.F.R. §493.1215 (Hematology)
rubrics_metrics.description: CMS determined that Theranos’ deficient practices in Hematology posed immediate jeopardy to patient health and safety under the condition-level requirement at 42 C.F.R. §493.1215.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finding of immediate jeopardy required Theranos to provide a credible allegation of compliance and acceptable evidence of correction within ten calendar days; failure led to revocation of CLIA certificates and civil monetary penalties before later settlement/abatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: FDA enforcement concern: shipping an uncleared medical device and incorrect device classification
rubrics_metrics.description: FDA inspection found Theranos shipped a capillary tube nanotainer that FDA identified as a Class II medical device while Theranos had identified it as Class I exempt, i.e., misclassification and shipment of an uncleared device in interstate commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misclassification and shipment without appropriate premarket submission can expose companies to enforcement actions; device class determines applicable regulatory controls and premarket requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: FDA Quality System (QS) failures — complaint handling, CAPA, software validation, supplier controls, records, device history, audits
rubrics_metrics.description: FDA cited systemic failures including lack of adequate procedures to evaluate complaints, failure to evaluate and document complaints, deficient documentation of corrective and preventive action (CAPA), missing software validation documentation, inadequate supplier evaluation and records, no proper device history procedures, and absent quality audits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These QS deficiencies reflect violations of device quality system/regulatory requirements and are common inspection triggers that demonstrate systemic compliance breakdowns; examples were used at trial to show knowledge of problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design validation and design control documentation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: FDA found Theranos’ design validation did not ensure the device conformed to defined user needs and intended uses, was not validated under actual or simulated use conditions, and design input requirements and design risk analysis were inadequately documented; important regulatory documents were not reviewed/approved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design validation under actual/simulated use, documented design inputs, risk analyses, and formal review/approval of hazard analyses are standard medical device requirements; failure can indicate a device was not properly established as safe/effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory analytical validity obligations under CLIA
rubrics_metrics.description: CLIA requires laboratories to establish performance characteristics assuring analytical validity for the use of a test system in the laboratory’s environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CMS enforcement focused on whether Theranos could demonstrate analytical validity (precision, bias, QC performance) of its proprietary instruments in its operating environment; failure undermined reliability of patient results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient impact assessment and obligation to notify affected patients
rubrics_metrics.description: Theranos’ internal patient impact assessment concluded possible patient impact for every test reported from proprietary instruments; although the lab voided results, it did not communicate the voiding to all affected patients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to notify patients of voided or potentially unreliable results is a serious patient-safety communication lapse and was illustrated by specific patient harms (false HIV, PSA, hCG results) used in the government’s case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of patient harm for sentencing enhancements
rubrics_metrics.description: Government argued patient harm justified sentencing enhancements for defendants; the court considered whether evidence showed conscious disregard of risk of death or serious bodily injury but declined enhancements in these cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentencing enhancements require specific findings (e.g., conscious disregard of risk); the court weighed evidence including that most samples were run on FDA-approved devices and limited direct evidence of patient injuries from the proprietary platform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of evidence about use of non-proprietary (FDA-approved) devices in assessing harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Court noted the majority of Theranos’ samples were run on other FDA-approved technology, not the Theranos platform, which influenced the assessment of patient-harm risk and sentencing decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing causation or magnitude of patient harm, whether unreliable testing was actually used on patients matters; prevalence of validated methods can mitigate findings about systemic patient risk from a proprietary platform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory corrective action process, appeals, and settlements (CMS path)
rubrics_metrics.description: CMS inspection led to a letter requiring corrective action, an unsuccessful response by Theranos, subsequent revocation of CLIA certificates, civil money penalties, and later a global settlement where revocation was withdrawn and civil penalty reduced in exchange for a lab operation ban for two years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency enforcement trajectories can include notices, opportunities to demonstrate correction, formal sanctions (revocation, penalties), appeals, and negotiated settlements that may alter initial enforcement outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility and use of FDA Form 483 and CMS reports as trial exhibits
rubrics_metrics.description: The government introduced redacted CMS reports and FDA Form 483 inspection observations to the jury; the court ruled such regulatory inspection reports were probative of defendants’ knowledge and state of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspection reports are evidentiary materials commonly used to show contemporaneous regulatory findings and can be influential in criminal/civil litigation to demonstrate awareness of problems, though courts may limit or redact portions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil and administrative liability exposures beyond criminal prosecution (SEC, state AG, corporate fallout)
rubrics_metrics.description: Separately from criminal charges, Holmes and Theranos settled an SEC complaint (penalty, share return, officer/director bar), Theranos settled state consumer-law claims, business relationships dissolved, and civil litigation ensued (e.g., Walgreens suit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misconduct around diagnostics can trigger multi-agency enforcement (SEC, CMS, FDA, state AG) and private-party suits, leading to financial penalties, corporate dissolution, bans, and injunctive remedies—risks companies should weigh alongside criminal exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecutorial strategy: preferring fraud charges over FDCA-based causes of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecutors chose to pursue wire fraud and conspiracy counts centered on misrepresentations because those allegations were simpler for a jury to understand than complex regulatory FDCA violations would have been.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When misconduct involves both regulatory noncompliance and deceptive statements, fraud charges may be tactically preferable due to clearer jury narratives; regulatory violations can still be used as supporting evidence of knowledge/intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public trust and agency enforcement messaging as regulatory considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: FDA’s public statements framed the prosecutions as protecting public trust in medical products and diagnostics and warned that individuals/companies putting public health at risk will be investigated and prosecuted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators’ public messaging after high-profile cases can influence industry expectations, spur legislative interest, and signal commitment to enforcement—companies should account for reputational/regulatory impacts beyond legal penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy implications for LDT oversight and the VALID Act proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: Theranos’ case was cited by stakeholders urging changes to oversight of laboratory-developed tests (LDTs); the VALID Act would establish a new risk-based pathway to regulate both LDTs (ICVTs) and commercial IVDs under a single framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: VALID has been proposed, debated, and reintroduced; it seeks to close perceived loopholes where high-risk tests could avoid FDA premarket review under CLIA; legislative progress or agency rulemaking could change the regulatory landscape for diagnostics.

rubrics_metrics.name: FDA administrative options in absence of legislation (rulemaking on LDTs)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of congressional action, FDA officials have indicated the agency would consider administrative options, including rulemaking, to impose additional requirements on LDTs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry should monitor both legislative initiatives (e.g., VALID) and possible agency rulemaking that could expand premarket/review requirements for tests developed and used within single laboratories.
